1: Chapter 1: A Visitor in the Rain
It had been raining on Pierrefeu for three days. In spring, Claire Martin's elder sister had left for Paris, and since then Claire had been running the village's small pharmacy alone.
Once night had fallen, she closed the shutters, counted the day's takings, blew out the lamp, and went upstairs.
She had scarcely lain down when someone knocked violently at the door downstairs. A man's voice asked, “Is anyone there?”
On the threshold stood a young man soaked to the bone, his left arm wrapped in a bloodstained cloth. He introduced himself: his name was Pierre Lapin, and he belonged to the Azure Dragon Society.
“I need you to treat me,” Lapin said quietly. “I can pay. Three thousand five hundred francs, will that be enough?”
He took a letter wrapped in oiled paper from his coat. “This letter must reach the abbey of Saint-Vent before the eighteenth of May.”
Since her sister had left, Claire had often felt blue in the evenings, but that night she did not have time to think about it.
Yet she refused his money and said only, “Tomorrow at dawn, I will take you into the mountains.”
2: At daybreak, they set out. Claire carried a basket on her back containing bread, medicinal herbs, and an old umbrella.

Halfway up the slope, they met old Gaston Roux, who was chopping wood. He set down his axe and told them in a low voice that, the previous evening, three strangers had questioned people at the village entrance about an injured young man.
“Take the path, my little Claire,” Gaston Roux said. “The main road isn’t safe.” Claire thanked him.
The path was narrow and slippery. Claire walked ahead, placing each step with confidence. Lapin followed her without a word.
At noon, the rain stopped; the mist slowly lifted, and the roof of the Saint-Vent abbey appeared in the distance. A nun, Sister Agnès, stood before the door, ready to welcome visitors.
Sister Agnès took the letter, examined the red seal, and nodded. “The abbess has been waiting for this letter for 2 years.”
Lapin said to Claire, “I owe you my life.” Claire smiled. “Then, next time, fix the roof of my pharmacy.” Lapin stayed at the abbey.
That evening, Claire descended the mountain alone. When she arrived home, it was already night; she lit the lamp and sat for a long time behind the counter.
